analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare to negotiate prescription drug prices directly with drug manufacturers.
analysis.headline: A bill to let Medicare negotiate drug prices, backed by 40 House Democrats, never got a committee vote and died when the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the 'non-interference' rule in Medicare Part D — the provision that bars the government from negotiating drug prices — and direct the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate prices, discounts, and rebates with drug manufacturers on behalf of the roughly 40 million seniors and disabled people enrolled in Part D drug plans. It would prohibit the Secretary from imposing a restrictive formulary and require semi-annual reports to Congress on the prices achieved.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare Part D beneficiaries — seniors and disabled people — would benefit if the negotiated prices lowered their premiums and out-of-pocket drug costs, and taxpayers would benefit because Medicare and the federal government fund the bulk of Part D spending.

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs the HHS Secretary to negotiate the prices, discounts, and rebates that drug manufacturers may charge Medicare Part D drug plans, replacing the current rule that prohibits the government from interfering in those negotiations.

It protects patients from supply-side coercion: the Secretary cannot establish or require a particular formulary, so the negotiation cannot be used to restrict access to covered drugs, and plans remain free to win discounts below the negotiated price.
The bill would take effect on enactment and first apply to plan years beginning January 1, 2014, and would require semi-annual reports to Congress on the prices achieved.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers would bear the cost, since government-negotiated prices, discounts, and rebates would cut the prices they charge on the large Medicare drug market.

drawbacks.text: Pharmaceutical manufacturers argue that government negotiation amounts to price-setting that would reduce industry revenue and could weaken the incentive to invest in developing new medicines — the reason the Part D statute originally barred government interference.
The bill directs the Secretary to negotiate but does not spell out enforcement or fallback mechanisms if manufacturers refuse to lower prices, leaving the actual savings uncertain.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is large: Medicare is one of the biggest drug buyers in the world, and other large purchasers negotiate, so even modest percentage reductions in Medicare drug prices would save beneficiaries and taxpayers billions. The main cost — some reduction in drug-industry revenues and possibly slower development of new drugs — is real but speculative in size, and the bill's prohibition on imposing a formulary guards against the most feared patient harm. The bill's main design weakness is that it mandates negotiation without specifying how to force a result if manufacturers hold firm.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and then to a Health subcommittee, where it sat; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter Welch introduced the bill on March 12, 2013, joined by 40 cosponsors, all Democrats.
The bill was referred to both the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, the two committees with jurisdiction over Medicare Part D.
Within days it was referred to the Health subcommittees of both committees, and no further action was ever recorded.
The bill expired without a vote when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015; bills not passed by the end of a Congress die and must be reintroduced.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers came out ahead: the existing Part D system, in which the government is barred from negotiating drug prices, stayed in place, and Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers continued paying the negotiated-nothing status quo. A similar negotiation bill (H.R. 3061) passed the House in 2007 but was never taken up by the Senate, so this mechanism has a track record of stalling rather than failing on a vote.

for.name: Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 40 cosponsors, all Democrats.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee (chair: Rep. Fred Upton, R-MI)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health subcommittee, which took no action; no hearing or markup was ever held.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee (chair: Rep. Dave Camp, R-MI)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health subcommittee, which took no action; no hearing or markup was ever held.

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers (industry)
against.role: Industry with an interest in keeping the negotiation ban
against.what_they_did: Opposed government negotiation of Medicare drug prices, consistent with the industry's long-standing defense of the Part D non-interference provision.

sides.party_line_note: All 40 cosponsors were Democrats and there were no Republican cosponsors; the Republican-controlled House committees never moved the bill.

industries.note: The bill would force manufacturers to accept government-negotiated prices, discounts, and rebates on Medicare Part D drugs — one of the largest drug-purchasing programs in the world. Keeping the ban on negotiation preserves their pricing power over Medicare beneficiaries, who pay through premiums and out-of-pocket costs.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D plan sponsors and Medicare Advantage insurers
industries.note: Negotiated lower prices would reduce what plans pay for covered drugs, potentially lowering premiums; the bill also lets plans bargain for discounts below the negotiated price. Their interests on this bill run alongside beneficiaries' interests.
